scope: local-only; no AWS writes; not browser Apply/Save/Reload proof

results.summary: The design covers the RL trading workflow end-to-end: historical training, simulation, continuous-action policy inference, regime conditioning, pre-trade risk controls, low-latency execution, and walk-forward evaluation with paper trading.

findings.title: Walk-forward gate strengthens risk-adjusted model promotion
findings.explanation: The design does more than train a policy; it requires walk-forward evaluation with multiple seeds, regime slices, and cost stress tests before promotion. That is a strong fit for a trading system where reward quality and overfitting control matter.

findings.title: Point-in-time replay supports reproducible research and paper trading
findings.explanation: Versioned market history, immutable replay into the simulator, and separate paper-mode persistence create a coherent research-to-paper workflow with replayable outcomes.

findings.title: Pre-trade risk service cleanly separates decision from execution
findings.explanation: The policy produces bounded proposals, the risk engine validates fresh state and limits, and only approved orders reach the execution adapter. This reduces unsafe direct-to-market exposure and improves control over live trading.

results.summary: The design is coherent and covers the core RL trading workflow, but the latency and backtest acceptance protocols remain underspecified, so the review needs clarification rather than a strong-alignment verdict.

findings.title: Strong end-to-end RL trading pipeline
findings.explanation: The design covers data ingestion, versioned replay, RL training, walk-forward evaluation, registry-based promotion, low-latency serving, pre-trade risk checks, execution, and monitoring in a coherent chain that matches the published core scope.

findings.title: Regime adaptation is explicitly modeled
findings.explanation: The separate regime detector and its use as an input to serving and evaluation provide a concrete mechanism for adapting behavior as market conditions change, rather than treating regime adaptation as an afterthought.

findings.title: Latency budget definition needs clarification
findings.explanation: The architecture shows a low-latency serving path, but it does not specify whether the under-10ms target is measured at model inference, full decision path, or order submission, and it does not break the budget down across serving, risk checks, and broker submission.
findings.recommendation: Clarify the latency measurement point and publish a budget allocation for serving, risk validation, and execution submission so the 10ms target is unambiguous.

findings.title: Backtest acceptance protocol needs clarification
findings.explanation: The walk-forward gate measures Sharpe and drawdown, but the submission does not state the exact fold construction rules, transaction-cost stress assumptions, or how borderline results are handled. The capability is present, but the evaluation contract is incomplete.
findings.recommendation: Document the walk-forward fold rules, cost-stress assumptions, and promotion thresholds so the backtest gate is reproducible and unambiguous.

results.summary: The architecture cleanly covers DAG orchestration, caching, lineage, retries, version control integration, and heterogeneous execution from ingest through deployment with a coherent replayable control plane.

findings.title: Immutable lineage and replay path is well covered
findings.explanation: The design captures the minimum metadata needed to reconstruct a prior run, including resolved parameters, source commit, dependency-lock revision, artifact digests, runtime identity, and stage attempts.

findings.title: Heterogeneous execution is explicitly modeled across CPU, GPU, and Spark
findings.explanation: The runtime separates control-plane orchestration from execution backends and includes dedicated paths for CPU preparation, Spark batch stages, and GPU training capacity.

findings.title: Content-addressed artifact handling supports cache hits and deduplication
findings.explanation: Prepared datasets, models, and cached artifacts are all referenced by immutable digests and checksums, which is aligned with both intermediate caching and storage deduplication.

results.summary: The architecture strongly covers DAG orchestration, lineage, caching, retries, distributed execution, and heterogeneous compute, but replay and cache lifecycle details remain operationally underspecified.

findings.title: Run replay mechanism is implied by lineage but not operationalized
findings.explanation: The design captures enough lineage to reconstruct a historical run, but it does not define the concrete replay entrypoint or orchestration flow. That leaves the user-facing replay behavior and reconstruction handoff ambiguous.
findings.recommendation: Define how a replay is triggered and which service rebuilds the pinned state from lineage records.

findings.title: Cache lifecycle beyond verified lookups is unspecified
findings.explanation: The cache keying and immutable-hit behavior support correctness, but eviction and refresh policy are not described. That makes the long-term cache behavior under churn an open design choice rather than a fully specified control.
findings.recommendation: Document cache eviction, refresh, and regeneration rules for stale or high-churn artifacts.

results.summary: The design covers batch and online serving, shared transformations, point-in-time joins, governance, and monitoring with a coherent offline/online architecture.

findings.title: Shared feature contract spans online and batch execution
findings.explanation: The versioned feature definition component is reused by both streaming and batch compute paths, which directly supports consistency and reduces skew risk.

findings.title: Point-in-time training data flow is explicit
findings.explanation: The design includes a dedicated PIT join that consumes historical offline data and governed schema/version metadata before feeding immutable training datasets.

findings.title: Governance and discovery are well integrated
findings.explanation: Discovery, documentation, authorization, ownership, lineage, and audit information are all centered in the metadata catalog and surfaced through the portal/API.

results.summary: Coherent feature-store architecture with strong coverage of training/inference, point-in-time joins, governance, and monitoring; the main gaps are unproven peak-load sizing, end-to-end throughput/latency strategy, and a few implementation-level operating decisions.

findings.title: Online serving capacity is not concretely sized for the published peak load
findings.explanation: The design includes an online cache and rate-limited API, but it does not specify partitioning, replication, cache cardinality, or other capacity decisions needed to show that the serving path can sustain 100k+ requests per second while keeping latency under 10ms.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit sharding/replication, locality, and cache sizing assumptions for the online path, and show how the API and cache remain within the latency budget under peak load.

findings.title: Scale strategy for 10k+ features across 100+ entities is implied but not demonstrated
findings.explanation: The catalog size is acknowledged, but the submission does not explain how metadata indexing, online cache partitioning, and materialization fan-out will behave as the feature set and entity count grow. That leaves the large-scale operating model under-specified.
findings.recommendation: Describe the partitioning and indexing approach for feature metadata and online values, plus how materialization and backfill workloads are distributed across the catalog size target.

findings.title: Peak-load compliance is not proven end-to-end
findings.explanation: The design states the 100k+ requests/second target at the gateway, but the downstream online feature lookup path is not specified in enough detail to show that the whole request chain can meet the published workload constraint under steady state and peak conditions.
findings.recommendation: Document the expected request path, cache hit strategy, and scaling assumptions for each hop so the end-to-end throughput target is credible.

findings.title: Implementation detail is still insufficient to make the solution directly buildable
findings.explanation: The architecture identifies the right components and flows, but some operational decisions remain abstract: for example, cache refresh policy, partitioning choices, and fallback behavior on missed online reads are not fully specified. That makes the design understandable but not fully prescriptive for implementation.
findings.recommendation: Add the missing operational decisions for hot-path retrieval, cache refresh/invalidation, and failure fallback so the implementation path is unambiguous.

results.summary: The design covers registry versioning, artifact and metadata storage, lifecycle promotion, lineage, comparison, CI/CD automation, RBAC, and auditability with coherent service boundaries and data flows.

findings.title: Event-driven promotion path is well-structured

findings.title: Version comparison and review are exposed clearly in the console

findings.title: Audit and lineage data are centralized in the metadata store
findings.explanation: The registry writes version manifests, metrics, lineage, approvals, and audit rows transactionally to one database, which simplifies traceability and consistent version history.

results.summary: The design comprehensively covers model versioning, artifact and metadata storage, lifecycle promotion, approval gating, lineage, metrics search, and CI/CD deployment with coherent component boundaries.

findings.title: Versioned registry and approval flow are well-aligned to the core scope
findings.explanation: The design cleanly separates registry metadata, artifact storage, identity checks, and event-driven promotion, which directly supports versioning, lifecycle management, approval, and automated deployment.

findings.title: Artifact and metadata separation is a strong fit for large model binaries
findings.explanation: Using an object store for immutable binaries and an RDBMS for manifests, metrics, lineage, and audit data is a coherent split for the stated 100GB artifact constraint and registry query needs.

results.summary: The design covers the registry, versioning, metadata, lifecycle, approval, lineage, CI/CD, and audit requirements with a coherent service split across registry, storage, database, identity, and pipeline components.

findings.title: Centralized metadata store supports version search and auditability
findings.explanation: The registry persists version manifests, indexed metrics, lineage, approvals, stage pointers, and audit rows in a transactional database, which directly supports the core registry behaviors and change history.

findings.title: Artifact and metadata split is cleanly separated
findings.explanation: Model binaries live in an immutable object store while metadata, lineage, and approvals remain in the database. This separation matches the different access patterns and makes the versioned registry easier to evolve.

findings.title: Approval and promotion path is explicit
findings.explanation: The design includes console review, registry authorization checks, persisted approvals, and an event-driven deployment trigger, forming a coherent promotion workflow.

results.summary: The design covers registry versioning, artifact and metadata storage, lifecycle promotion, approval, lineage, metric search/comparison, CI/CD integration, RBAC, and auditability with coherent component and connection choices.

findings.title: Immutable registry and promotion path is well separated
findings.explanation: Version creation, approval, lifecycle transition, and deployment are split across the registry, identity, database, event bus, and pipeline, which makes the control flow understandable and auditable.

findings.title: Metric comparison and lineage review are explicitly exposed in the console
findings.explanation: The UI flow covers the requested operator tasks rather than leaving them implicit, including version search, side-by-side comparison, model cards, lineage review, and approval actions.

results.summary: The design cleanly covers registry versioning, artifact storage, lifecycle promotion, lineage, approval, and CI/CD integration with a coherent set of services and data flows.

findings.title: Immutable versioning and lifecycle ownership are centralized in the registry service
findings.explanation: The Model Registry Service owns immutable version IDs, metadata, stage transitions, approval policy, and exact-digest aliases, which is the right responsibility split for this domain.

findings.title: Artifact, lineage, and audit data are persisted transactionally
findings.explanation: The metadata database stores version manifests, indexed metrics, lineage, approvals, audit rows, and an outbox, giving the design a coherent source of truth for registry state and history.

findings.title: Version comparison and model-card review are explicitly supported in the UI
findings.explanation: The console and API flow includes version search, side-by-side comparison, model-card review, lineage review, and approval actions, which directly addresses the review workflow needs.

results.summary: The design has a coherent end-to-end monitoring and retraining flow, with strong drill-down and archival support, but it still needs explicit drift-test selection and text-feature handling to fully satisfy the brief.

findings.title: Drift detection method is implied but not explicitly specified
findings.explanation: The evaluator compares sliding-window summaries with versioned reference distributions, but the design does not identify the statistical tests or selection criteria used to decide whether a drift event is significant. That leaves the exact mechanism for requirement 4 partially unspecified.
findings.recommendation: Name the drift tests and decision policy, for example per-feature KS/chi-square/proportion tests with calibrated thresholds and multiple-testing handling.

findings.title: Text-feature handling is not explicit
findings.explanation: The brief requires support for numerical, categorical, and text features, but the architecture only explicitly shows a versioned feature store and feature evidence. It does not describe how text is tokenized, embedded, or compared for drift.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit text-feature representation and drift strategy, such as text embeddings or token-distribution summaries with versioned preprocessing.

results.summary: A coherent distributed training platform is defined end-to-end: durable job intake, elastic multi-node scheduling, sharded input, parallel training, checkpointed recovery, and observability are all present and connected.

findings.title: Distributed training path is fully articulated across scheduling, input, execution, and recovery
findings.explanation: The submitted design links job admission, durable queueing, elastic placement, sharded input, distributed runtime execution, checkpoint persistence, and observability into a coherent end-to-end training workflow.

findings.title: Recovery loop is explicitly closed with durable manifesting and verified restore
findings.explanation: The system records only complete checkpoint manifests, keeps checkpoint shards immutable and checksummed, and restores restarted attempts from the committed manifest. That is a strong failure-handling pattern for distributed training.

findings.title: Metrics cover both training efficiency and fleet health
findings.explanation: The observability path captures throughput, GPU use, memory, input stalls, collectives, checkpoint overhead, placement events, and node/fabric health, which is well matched to diagnosing throughput and starvation problems.

results.summary: A coherent distributed-training platform design with elastic scheduling, sharded input, mixed-precision runtime support, durable checkpoint recovery, and comprehensive operational telemetry.

findings.title: End-to-end distributed training path is well decomposed
findings.explanation: The submission cleanly separates admission, scheduling, data loading, distributed execution, checkpointing, and observability. That makes the training workflow understandable and implementable without overloading a single component.

findings.title: Recovery path is explicitly checkpoint-manifest driven
findings.explanation: The design uses durable run state plus a complete checkpoint manifest before resume, which is a strong fault-tolerance pattern for distributed training jobs.

findings.title: Observability includes training, queue, and fleet signals
findings.explanation: The monitoring component collects throughput, GPU use, input stalls, collectives, queue age, resize events, and hardware health, which is the right operational surface for this platform.

results.summary: The design provides a coherent elastic distributed training platform with data/model parallel runtime support, durable scheduling, bounded input prefetch, checkpoint-based recovery, and operational telemetry across jobs, GPUs, and checkpoints.

findings.title: Coherent end-to-end distributed training control plane
findings.explanation: The design links job admission, durable queuing, elastic scheduling, GPU allocation, input delivery, runtime execution, checkpointing, and observability into one consistent flow. That makes the architecture understandable and directly aligned to the brief.

findings.title: Checkpoint recovery path is well-structured
findings.explanation: The design persists checkpoint shards immutably, records only complete manifests, and restores from verified checkpoint references. This is a strong reliability pattern for interrupted training jobs.

findings.title: Runtime and observability coupling supports operational diagnosis
findings.explanation: The runtime emits step, memory, communication, and input-stall measurements while the observability layer correlates them with GPU, queue, node, and checkpoint health. That is appropriate for a distributed training platform.

results.summary: The submission provides a coherent distributed training platform with elastic multi-node scheduling, parallel training support, durable checkpoint recovery, sharded input, and operational visibility across the full training lifecycle.

findings.title: Strong end-to-end distributed training path
findings.explanation: The design connects job admission, durable queueing, elastic placement, sharded input, distributed runtime execution, checkpoint persistence, and observability in a coherent flow that matches the published scope.

findings.title: Elastic scheduling is aligned with the scale target
findings.explanation: Gang placement, elastic resize policy, and scheduler-managed GPU fleet allocation are appropriate for the 100+ GPU constraint and the need to change cluster membership dynamically.

results.summary: The design presents a coherent distributed training platform with elastic multi-node scheduling, parallel training support, sharded input prefetching, checkpoint-based recovery, and broad observability aligned to the published core scope.

findings.title: Distributed training stack is coherent across scheduling, data, runtime, checkpointing, and observability
findings.explanation: The submitted design ties together job admission, priority scheduling, elastic GPU allocation, sharded input delivery, distributed execution, durable checkpoints, and operational telemetry in a way that directly matches the published core scope.

findings.title: Elastic checkpoint recovery path is explicitly modeled
findings.explanation: The design uses immutable checkpoint shards, a committed manifest, and restart-time restore from the verified checkpoint store, which is the right pattern for failure recovery in distributed training.

findings.title: Operational telemetry covers the main training bottlenecks
findings.explanation: The observability component receives metrics for throughput, GPU utilization, input stalls, collectives, queue age, node health, and checkpoint overhead, giving operators the signals needed to diagnose starvation and scaling issues.

results.summary: The design presents a coherent model-serving platform with REST/gRPC ingress, canary and A/B traffic routing, autoscaling from volume and latency, multi-framework serving, batching, warm-up/preloading, and monitoring.

findings.title: Strong coverage of the full serving and rollout flow
findings.explanation: The design covers API exposure, version resolution, artifact loading, stable/candidate serving pools, canary/A-B routing, autoscaling, and monitoring in a connected flow.

findings.title: Readiness-gated routing supports zero-downtime releases
findings.explanation: Candidate traffic is only enabled after readiness is established, and stable traffic remains available during rollout, which is the right architectural pattern for uninterrupted deployment changes.

findings.title: Monitoring loop is sufficient for autoscaling signals
findings.explanation: Request volume and latency are collected centrally and fed back to the orchestrator, giving a coherent control loop for reactive scaling decisions.

results.summary: The design covers the published serving, rollout, autoscaling, batching, warm-up, observability, and multi-framework requirements with a coherent split between routing, model pools, registry/storage, and autoscaling control.

findings.title: Explicit canary and A/B traffic control is well separated from model execution
findings.explanation: The design cleanly isolates traffic policy in the router and keeps serving pools focused on model execution, which reduces coupling and makes rollout policy changes easier to reason about.

findings.title: Autoscaling is driven by the same signals used for operational visibility
findings.explanation: Request volume and latency are collected in monitoring and fed to the orchestrator, creating a coherent feedback loop for scaling decisions.

findings.title: Candidate and stable pools share the same framework and readiness contract
findings.explanation: Using parallel stable and candidate pools with the same framework support, batching, and readiness behavior is a strong fit for canary and A/B comparisons.

results.summary: The design cleanly covers serving, canary/A/B routing, autoscaling, multi-framework support, and observability, but it under-specifies the high-load control path and the enforcement details needed to prove the stated constraints.

findings.title: Capacity strategy is directionally sound but under-specified for extreme throughput
findings.explanation: The design includes REST/gRPC endpoints, a router, and autoscaling, but it does not show a concrete overload strategy such as queue shaping, backpressure, or admission control for the 50k+ RPS target. That leaves the high-load path partially unproven.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit high-traffic control path, such as bounded queues, backpressure, or request shedding, and describe how the router and autoscaler behave under saturation.

findings.title: Latency target lacks an explicit p99 protection mechanism
findings.explanation: The architecture monitors latency and uses it for scaling, but it does not specify how request batching, readiness gating, or routing policy will keep inference p99 below 100ms during load spikes.
findings.recommendation: State the batching policy, queue bounds, and any latency-based routing or shedding thresholds used to protect the p99 target.

findings.title: Constraint bundle is only partially demonstrated
findings.explanation: The submission acknowledges the core constraints, but it does not fully demonstrate compliance for the p99 under-100ms target or the sub-30-second model loading target. The architecture has the right ingredients, yet the actual enforcement mechanism and timing path remain unspecified.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit latency and loading budgets, plus the mechanism that enforces them in routing, batching, and model warm-up.

results.summary: The design covers multi-source ingestion, stage-wise validation, schema evolution, dataset versioning, quality reporting, and training gates with a coherent queue-to-worker-to-store flow.

findings.title: Durable, gated ingestion-to-training path
findings.explanation: The design cleanly separates source ingestion, validation, versioned storage, feature publication, and downstream training release gating, which makes the end-to-end flow easy to reason about and aligns well with the published scope.

findings.title: Strong schema-evolution handling
findings.explanation: Versioned data contracts with compatibility rules and reviewed migration for breaking changes directly address the need for schema consistency and evolution without interrupting the pipeline.

findings.title: Good operational visibility through existing components
findings.explanation: Monitoring, warehouse-backed reports, and the report workspace together provide stage status, quality findings, and lineage context without introducing unnecessary extra services.

results.summary: AI review is unavailable. This is a basic structural check of submitted identifiers and endpoints, not an architecture assessment. Numeric fields are compatibility placeholders, not design feedback.

findings.title: Full architecture review unavailable
findings.explanation: The design has not been evaluated against required scope.
findings.recommendation: Retry the AI review when the service is available.

findings.title: Peak-load compliance is not proven end-to-end
findings.explanation: The design states the 100k+ requests/second target at the gateway, but the downstream online feature lookup path is not specified in enough detail to show that the whole request chain can meet the published workload constraint under steady state and peak conditions.
findings.recommendation: Document the expected request path, cache hit strategy, and scaling assumptions for each hop so the end-to-end throughput target is credible.

findings.title: Implementation detail is still insufficient to make the solution directly buildable
findings.explanation: The architecture identifies the right components and flows, but some operational decisions remain abstract: for example, cache refresh policy, partitioning choices, and fallback behavior on missed online reads are not fully specified. That makes the design understandable but not fully prescriptive for implementation.
findings.recommendation: Add the missing operational decisions for hot-path retrieval, cache refresh/invalidation, and failure fallback so the implementation path is unambiguous.

findings.title: Constraint bundle is only partially demonstrated

findings.recommendation: Add explicit latency and loading budgets, plus the mechanism that enforces them in routing, batching, and model warm-up.
